title: What County Am I In? Census-Verified Counties
description: Answer 'What County Am I In?' with Census verification — FIPS code, boundary check and ACS context for US points; mapped data elsewhere. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a point in Chicago resolves to Cook County, FIPS 17031 — verified against Census county geometry, the same key that unlocks the county's ACS estimates.
quick_answer: What County Am I In? verifies a US point against U.S. Census county geometry and returns the county, its FIPS code and recent ACS context. Use GPS, search an address, paste coordinates or click the map; outside the US it falls back to mapped administrative data where available.

body.t: Cook County 17031, Harris County 48201, Los Angeles County 06037: five digits, state plus county, unique nationwide. Names repeat across states — 'Washington County' exists in 31 of them; the code never repeats.
Louisiana parishes, Alaska boroughs, Virginia's independent cities: the Census treats them as county-equivalents and so does this page.

faq: How are U.S. county results verified?
The point is tested against U.S. Census Bureau county geometry — a point-in-polygon check against the official shapes, which is how the FIPS code attached can be trusted.
Does the tool work outside the United States?
Yes, via mapped administrative-area data where available — county-equivalents such as districts and regions. The Census verification and FIPS are US-only, and the page labels the difference.
Where do U.S. demographics come from?
The U.S. Census Bureau's American Community Survey (ACS) — recent estimates joined by FIPS. They are estimates with margins of error, published as context, exactly as the Census intends.
Can I use GPS, an address or coordinates?
All three, plus a map click — every route resolves to the same verified check on the same point.
Is this suitable for legal boundary decisions?
It is a strong first answer — Census geometry is the public standard. Legal determinations belong to official authorities and surveys.
What is a FIPS code?
The Federal Information Processing Standards code: two digits for the state, three for the county — the universal key for US county data.
Independent cities?
Virginia's independent cities (and a few elsewhere) are county-equivalents with their own FIPS — handled as counties, correctly.
The point is in water.
Census geometry includes county water areas in places (the Great Lakes especially) — a water point can legitimately return the county whose water it is.
County changed its boundary?
Annexations and rare reorganisations happen; Census vintages track them. The geometry here follows a stated Census vintage.
County seats and courthouses?
Beyond the county's identity, its seat is a separate lookup in the county's own records. This page's FIPS unlocks those datasets.
Two counties claim the point?
Point-in-polygon against one geometry set gives one verdict. Where sources disagree, it is vintage — and the Census set is the reference this page stands on.
